sources.text: Skip to content I n selling its blockbuster anticancer drug Keytruda to the Russian government, the pharmaceutical giant Merck turned to a hospital supplier with friends in high places: Alexey Repik, a now-sanctioned oligarch close to Russian President Vladimir Putin and fluent in the ways of Russia and Western business. A native of Moscow, trained as an economist, Repik started R-Pharm in 2001 after selling his car and borrowing $15,000 from his mother. Serving as an intermediary for pharmaceutical firms bidding on massive government contracts for medicine, the firm took off. In 2009, the year New Jersey-based Merck forged a strategic alliance with R-Pharm, the Russian company was expanding and soon teamed up with other Western firms and formed new lines of business. Repik amassed billions of dollars, a mansion in San Francisco and a precious collection of modern art and Japanese prints. He enjoyed high-stakes poker events at luxury casino hotels in the West, joining high-roller pros and gaining a reputation as a somewhat aggressive and unorthodox player. And he attracted scrutiny. Some in the media questioned whether insider connections to government officials helped him win contracts. Repik brushed off the question. “In the classical sense, no,” he said in a 2015 interview. “Officials and shadow leaders have never stood behind us.” R-Pharm also faced scrutiny from Russia’s Federal Antimonopoly Service, which investigated whether the firm coordinated bidding with other medicine distributors and in separate cases engaged in anticompetitive conduct designed to maintain high drug prices and influence winners. Yet R-Pharm kept growing, deepening its relationship with Merck by sharing manufacturing know-how and producing medicines jointly. Along the way, Repik became a political heavyweight. He met one-on-one with Putin, was invited to mingle with the super elite at the World Economic Forum and attended Donald Trump’s first presidential inauguration festivities in 2017. The oligarch bragged on Facebook that he was able to “check the handshake strength” of the president-elect. And news investigations later found that an offshore company linked to Repik owned a Bombardier business jet apparently used by one of Putin’s daughters. Alexey Repik’s Facebook post from the U.S. election night in 2016 shows him in a red Make America Great Again hat, giving a thumbs up. The series explores strategies that pharmaceutical firms use to maintain multibillion-dollar monopolies and to keep cancer drug prices high — at the expense of patients and depleted healthcare resources around the world. sources.title: How Beijing's Africa ambitions, financed by China's mega banks, triggered a crisis in Zambia - ICIJ
sources.text: Skip to content CHINA CAPITAL How Beijing’s Africa ambitions, financed by China’s mega banks, triggered a crisis in Zambia Chinese banking giants piled loans onto the debt-ridden country, then adopted a hardball stance when it came time to repay, documents show. By Micah Reddy Image: Ben King / ICIJ / Getty Images October 26, 2026 A s Kanangwa Newlove walked through her 10-acre farm just outside Lusaka, Zambia, one day in October 2025, she felt as if her dreams were withering away in front of her. The spinach, lettuce and mustard wilted in the heat. Tomatoes shriveled on their vines. She uprooted entire rows of organic vegetables — once sought-after by discerning customers, now rotting in the sun — and fed them to her pigs. “The crops that suffered the most without water were our mainstay,” she told a reporter for the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists. “There was nothing we could do. There was no water for the crops because there was no electricity.” Every few days, she needed nearly 8,000 gallons of water from borehole pumps to keep her farm going. The pumps required a reliable supply of electricity, but since March 2024, Zambia’s rolling blackouts had left swathes of the country without power, turning everyday tasks into Herculean struggles. Sometimes she had only four hours of power a day. The blackouts had a “cascading effect,” Newlove said. Without electricity she couldn’t refrigerate the few meager vegetables she could harvest. She stopped breeding and slaughtering animals. She was unable to sell to many of her regular customers, like local “mom and pop shops.” She had to drastically reduce the area she farmed and cut back on planting, and she couldn’t hire seasonal workers. The rolling blackouts affecting Newlove’s farm were a result of “load shedding,” scheduled power cuts meant to reduce demand on the grid. ZESCO, the state-owned power company supplying almost all of Zambia’s energy needs, alerted its customers to the load shedding schedule, but these schedules weren’t consistent or reliable, Newlove told ICIJ, making it hard to plan how to maintain — or save — her crops. “One week you’d get a schedule from, say, morning to midday and you’d make a plan based on that,” she said. “Then, without prior notice, it would change.” She couldn’t run a farm on four hours of electricity. For the first time since she’d started the farm over a decade earlier — a labor of love she launched while working for a social enterprise — she began to wonder if she’d need to shut it down. “Farmers are optimistic people until that is obliterated entirely by reality. … It’s a mammoth thing to fathom, that you’re going to kill a business that you’ve worked so hard for for so many years,” she said. Kanangwa Newlove started farming just outside Lusaka in 2012, selling organic produce to local businesses. Image: Micah Reddy / ICIJ Newlove and other small-business owners across Zambia faced collapse amid a perfect storm in which environmental and economic shocks were exacerbated by the country’s deep-seated financial problems. Zambia — where roughly 60% of the population lives in poverty — is overwhelmingly dependent on hydropower, but a severe drought in 2024 left dams empty and forced ZESCO to ration electricity usage. While Zambia is drought-prone, ZESCO’s financial woes left it uniquely ill-prepared for the drought, the worst in decades. The company was sinking financially. Among its biggest expenses was a long-term loan of nearly $285 million from the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) with tough repayment terms. The loan was signed more than a decade before, in 2011, and in the following years, ZESCO had taken on more and more debt from ICBC and other Chinese lenders. Beholden to Chinese creditors, the power utility mirrored Zambia, one of the world’s most indebted countries and the first in Africa to default on its sovereign debt during the COVID-19 pandemic. sources.title: Tax Filing: IRS Should Enhance Ghost Preparer Identification and Compliance Efforts in a Comprehensive Preparer Strategy | U.S. GAO
sources.text:
Tax Filing: IRS Should Enhance Ghost Preparer Identification and Compliance Efforts in a Comprehensive Preparer Strategy | U.S. GAO Skip to main content GAO-27-108176 Published: Oct 15, 2026. Publicly Released: Oct 16, 2026.
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who hide their identities on returns and avoid accountability for making errors, committing fraud, or stealing refunds. But ghost preparers are hard for IRS to identify—leaving taxpayers responsible for errors or fraud.
The IRS has started addressing this problem, but its efforts are fragmented. For example, relevant data is scattered across several databases. This makes it hard for IRS to use this information to better understand ghost preparer behavior and protect taxpayers.
IRS also doesn't have a strategy, goals, or ways to measure the success of its efforts.
Our recommendations address these issues.
A pen points to the paid preparer section of a tax return.
Ghost preparers are paid tax preparers who do not comply with requirements to identify themselves on tax returns they prepare for others. Ghost preparers may intentionally leave identifying information off to get away with filing fraudulent income tax returns, stealing taxpayers’ refunds, and stealing taxpayers’ identities. Courts have ordered individual ghost preparers to pay millions in restitution to the government, but according to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) officials, the total effect of ghost preparers is likely greater, in part, because ghost preparers are difficult to detect.
IRS maintains some data on identified ghost preparers, but the systems IRS uses to track ghost preparer cases and outcomes are not connected and have limitations that impede their usefulness. As a result, IRS does not know how many ghost preparers it has identified, investigated, and addressed. Better understanding existing data, including its limitations, would help IRS direct enforcement resources and protect taxpayers from fraudulent returns or stolen refunds.
IRS identifies and addresses ghost preparers through data analysis, referrals, taxpayer education, and enforcement actions such as investigations. However, these efforts are fragmented across six offices and IRS is missing opportunities to share information and better address risks. A comprehensive, coordinated preparer strategy, including efforts addressing ghost preparers, could help IRS better align resources with risks and identify additional needs.
Notional Example of Fragmented Activities Compared to a Comprehensive, Coordinated Strategy
While IRS has some activities to address ghost preparers, including data analysis and taxpayer education, it has not developed measurable objectives or performance goals. Defining objectives, goals, and performance measures could help IRS reliably assess whether its efforts are reducing ghost preparer activity and adjust its strategy and allocate resources more effectively.
Paid tax preparers prepared more than half of all tax returns in fiscal year 2025 and have an enormous effect on IRS’s ability to administer tax laws effectively. However, ghost preparers may hide their identities to avoid accountability and leave taxpayers responsible for inaccurate or fraudulent returns they prepare.
GAO was asked to examine IRS’s efforts to address ghost preparers. This report (1) describes how ghost preparers have harmed taxpayers and IRS, (2) assesses the extent to which IRS maintains data on ghost preparers, and (3) evaluates IRS actions to identify and address ghost preparers.
GAO reviewed federal court cases, and IRS documentation and data. GAO compared IRS’s efforts to leading practices for evidence-based policymaking and consumer education planning. GAO also interviewed IRS and Department of Justice officials and stakeholder groups, such as IRS oversight and industry groups.

sources.title: Ciara Mageean: Funeral of Olympian takes place - BBC News
sources.text:
Image source, Press Association Image caption, Ciara Mageean's funeral took place in Portaferry, County Down By Cormac Campbell BBC News NI south east reporter Published 3 November 2026, 16:20 GMT
Olympian Ciara Mageean has been described as a "truly remarkable, immensely talented and inspirational human being" in a tribute read out at her funeral.
Hundreds of people have paid their respects to the runner at her funeral on Tuesday.
The former European champion and two-time Olympic runner died on Sunday after she was diagnosed with stage four bowel cancer.
Among those in attendance at the funeral in Portaferry, County Down, were Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill, as well as fellow Olympian Rhys McClenaghan and 1972 gold medallist Lady Mary Peters.
Mageean's funeral cortege was given a guard of honour by Portaferry GAC and her former school, Assumption Grammar in Ballynahinch.
Image source, Pacemaker Her death comes less than three weeks after her marriage to her long-term partner Thomas Moran.
Mourners began arriving at around midday for the 2:00 GMT requiem Mass at St Patrick's Church.
Family, friends and those wishing to pay their respects followed the funeral cortege the short distance along the Ballyphilip Road from Mageean's family home to the church.
Others in attendance included representatives for Irish President Catherine Connolly and the Irish Government, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader Claire Hanna, GAA President Jarlath Burns and former boxer Paddy Barnes.
Image source, PA Image caption, European champion Ciara Mageean died surrounded by her loved ones at the weekend
The Mass booklet included an image of Mageean's greatest achievement on the track, the moment she crossed the line at the 2024 European Championships.
In his homily, Father Martin Kelly, who knew Mageean from her childhood, spoke of her accomplishments, her love for her husband and the joy and pride she had brought to her hometown.
Kelly recalled visiting her in hospice shortly before her death, when she suggested they go for a walk.
Despite her illness, Mageean noticed he was struggling and offered to link arms with him.
"On the way down, she knew I was struggling and she said, 'Let me link you'," he told mourners.
"One of my happiest moments and memories is that of Ciara Mageean linking my arm as we walked back to her room."
The athlete represented Ireland at the 2016 and 2020 Olympics and won gold in the 1500m at the European Athletics Championships in Rome in 2024.
She also represented Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, winning silver in Birmingham in 2022.
Noticing blood in your poo - which may appear black or dark red in the toilet bowl - can be a sign of bowel cancer.
If there is no other obvious cause for the bleeding, such as piles, the NHS recommends that you ask for an appointment with your GP , external .
The NHS also advises a check-up if you notice changes in your regular toilet habits, such as having to poo more often, or a pattern of diarrhoea or constipation.
Abdominal pain or lumps, stomach bloating and unexplained weight loss are also among symptoms which should lead to a bowel cancer test.
Bowel cancer can also cause anaemia, the features of which include extreme tiredness and shortness of breath.
The earlier bowel cancer is detected, the easier it is to treat.

sources.title: Benetton sells 900,000 hectares of farmland to Adecoagro executives | Buenos Aires Times
sources.text:
A group of partners and executives from agricultural firm Adecoagro has acquired two businesses belonging to the Benetton family's holding company in a deal involving more than 900,000 hectares of land across four Argentine provinces.
The transaction effectively marks the end of the Italian family's 35-year presence in Argentina, where it built up a major agricultural and livestock business.
The Benettons were among Argentina's largest landowners, with holdings that placed them prominently on rankings of the country's biggest private landholders. Their vast Patagonian estates have featured in debates over land ownership and foreign investment in Argentina.
Mariano Bosch, Adecoagro's chief executive, led the acquisition of Compañía de Tierras Sud and Ganadera Cóndor, a deal that had been in the works for around a year, sources close to the transaction confirmed to the Noticias Argentinas (NA) news agency.
The purchase was made by the investors in their individual capacity, rather than by Adecoagro itself, reported NA. The agency said Agustín Dranovsky would remain on as CEO of Compañía de Tierras Sud.
The two companies operate agricultural and livestock establishments in the provinces of Buenos Aires, Río Negro, Chubut and Santa Cruz, with activities focused primarily on sheep farming, wool production and agriculture.
The Patagonian operation comprises around 250,000 sheep and produce more than 880,000 kilos of wool, according to reports. In Buenos Aires Province, the agricultural business grows potatoes, maize and wheat.
Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino was the main vehicle through which the Benetton family developed its Argentine agricultural and livestock operations under the Edizione holding group.
The family acquired the company in 1991, when it held around 360,000 hectares across the Leleque, Maitén, Pilcaniyeu and Montoso estates in Chubut and Río Negro.
The companies have also operated in cattle farming, forestry and meat processing.
The sale comes amid Adecoagro's wider expansion. The company recently joined the Asociación de Cooperativas Argentinas (ACA) in acquiring fertiliser producer Profertil in a deal valued at US$1.2 billion.
Adecoagro was not directly involved in the Benetton transaction. Its value and terms were not disclosed, NA reported.

sources.title: A reclusive billionaire, a ‘fearless’ dealer and a globe-spanning feud over priceless art - ICIJ
sources.text: Skip to content Before everything turned sour, Russian billionaire Dmitry Rybolovlev and Swiss art world figure Yves Bouvier had a flourishing partnership. Bouvier, a self-proclaimed “fearless” wheeler-dealer, was pioneering the freeport model — a kind of free-trade zone for art, where the ultra wealthy could stash and trade expensive pieces without the art ever leaving the building. Rybolovlev, a reclusive potash mogul and art collector, was looking to expand his portfolio — and Bouvier was happy to help. For more than a decade, Bouvier worked to help Rybolovlev amass one of the world’s great art collections. Then, their relationship fell apart. Their globe-spanning, multi-billion-dollar feud is at the heart of “ The Oligarch and the Art Dealer ,” a new documentary from Danish director Andreas Dalsgaard, which dives deep into the shadowy trade in priceless masterpieces. The film explores the series of lawsuits, criminal cases (that were eventually dropped), dirty tricks-style surveillance operations, and dramatic press coverage that played out after Rybolovlev accused Bouvier of swindling at least $1 billion by lying about the purchase prices of major works and pocketing the difference. (After a drawn-out battle, Rybolovlev and Bouvier eventually settled their dispute, with the terms undisclosed.) It also draws on ICIJ’s Panama Papers investigation, which helped expose how Bouvier used a vast network of offshore companies to move billions of dollars worth of art for his many clients, including Rybolovlev. The film is showing as part of the Double Exposure Investigative Film Festival and Forum in Washington, D.C. this week. ICIJ spoke with Dalsgaard about how art has become one of the most efficient vehicles for hiding huge amounts of wealth, the challenges of documenting a billionaire oligarch, and how certain U.S. states have become magnets for dark money. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Let’s start with the oligarch of the title of the film. You interviewed people who worked with Dmitry Rybolovlev. He’s a major part of the film, but ultimately, he’s not really there to speak for himself. What kind of character is he to you, beyond just a Russian oligarch? What was unique in this story is that he never talks – literally never. He’s made one very short interview about the AES Monaco Football Club that he owns. That’s pretty much it. The story is about the dispute between the oligarch Rybolovlev and the Swiss art dealer and freeport magnate Bouvier. And they’ve been fighting it out in courts in eight countries. They’ve had PR teams. They’ve had spies. So much has been made available to the public and to us through these court cases, everything from years of emails, years of text messages, invoices, whatnot. And to be allowed to look into a world they occupy — which is both the world of the ultra rich and the top echelon of the art market — and see how those deals were made, see how those negotiations take place, see how they communicate with each other, it’s just unique. I don’t know of any other case where that’s been so accessible. It’s very interesting to me about how art stops being art. sources.title: Western Pharma Giants Paid Millions to Russian Distributors Linked to Fraud, Whistleblower Report Says - The Moscow Times
sources.text:
Four major Western pharmaceutical companies paid tens of millions of dollars in unusually high bonuses to Russian middlemen to supply cancer drugs to state hospitals, according to whistleblower documents submitted to U.S. financial regulators.
The payments by Merck, Eli Lilly, Novartis and AstraZeneca allegedly helped fund a corruption scheme that kept drug prices high and limited competition across Russia’s public healthcare system.
The pharmaceutical companies were alleged to have provided “excessive” sales bonuses and rebates ranging from 15% to 35% to Russian distributors, with the international average rarely exceeding 10%.
The whistleblower report and other details were laid out in a joint investigation published Monday by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), the exiled Russian news outlet Proekt and the Swiss publication Republik.
According to the report, Merck’s Russian distributor R-Pharma won $360 million in state contracts for the cancer drug Keytruda, winning 2,400 out of nearly 5,000 bids between 2020 and 2022. Procurement data reportedly showed 96% of the bids had no competitors, allowing sanctioned oligarch Alexei Repik’s R-Pharm to maintain a virtual monopoly on Keytruda supplies to state hospitals.
R-Pharm CEO Vasily Ignatyev denied “any involvement” in improper payments or non-competitive practices, telling ICIJ that its commercial rebates were legitimate and defending Russia’s state auction procedures as transparent.
Separately, Eli Lilly was alleged to have budgeted a 34% bonus for sales of its advanced cancer drug Cyramza in 2022. The year before, Moscow’s health department awarded more than $5 million in Cyramza contracts to distributor Pharmstandard, the sole bidder for most of those contracts.
In another example, AstraZeneca’s drug Tagrisso was sold to Russian state hospitals at or above its official list price of at least $3,000 per box after single-participant bids in 95% of state tenders between 2020 and 2023. The company used distributor Pharmimex, which won $114.3 million out of nearly $129 million in state contracts for another drug, Koselugo, between 2022 and 2024 without competition.
AstraZeneca, Merck and Eli Lilly either declined to comment or did not respond to requests from ICIJ for comment.
Novartis, a Swiss multinational pharmaceutical corporation, was alleged to have identified examples of bid-rigging in government auctions for the drug Kisqali by distributors like Pharmimex and their affiliated front companies.
A Novartis representative said the company conducted an internal investigation into the allegations without disclosing its findings.
While the whistleblower reports do not contain direct financial records of bank transfers between distributors and officials, they allege that Western drugmakers were “willfully blind” to how their profit margins were being used.
U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act holds parent companies legally responsible for ignoring signs that third-party distributors are using company margins to fund kickbacks.
The SEC and the Justice Department both declined to comment on the filings to ICIJ.

“There’s going to be an agreement. It’s going to be a big agreement, and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” Trump said, adding that the effort could include “all of Europe”.
Trump has frequently predicted that an agreement to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II was close. Negotiations have, however, picked up in recent weeks.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came after a diplomatic gathering hosted by First Lady Melania Trump, which brought Russian and Ukrainian representatives together to mark and build on the localised six-day truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October. The US president did not attend the event.
The temporary ceasefire ran from October 27 to November 1 and allowed for the evacuation of nearly 800 civilians from the besieged, Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Ukraine’s Kherson region, as well as the delivery of critical food and medical supplies.
Senior officials from both countries attended on Thursday, including Dmitriev; Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner; David Arakhamia, leader of the Servant of the People party in Ukraine’s parliament; and Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s parliamentary human rights commissioner.
Melania Trump also spoke at the event, which the White House described as “the first time in American history that a First Lady has personally brought representatives of two nations at war to the White House for diplomacy”.
“Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire,” she said, urging both sides to see the humanitarian truce in Oleshky “as a spark in a world of darkness”.

The tankers reportedly departed from the Baltic Sea port of Primorsk last month and had declared their destinations as the US east coast.
This all comes after US President Donald Trump eased sanctions on Russian oil last month , in a deal with with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to secure a large amount of diesel directly to the US at a time when diesel prices have skyrocketed across the country.
The agreement caused shock and drew criticism in Ukraine and Europe. But it also was a logistical challenge, given that sanctions against Russia still remain in place.
It was also widely reported at the time that the amount of diesel in question was a fraction of the US daily demand.
UK newspaper The Financial Times (FT) reported Wednesday that two of the tankers appeared to have changed their destination and were no longer headed to the United States.
Russian envoy and negotiator Kirill Dmitriev said on Thursday that the US-bound diesel tankers were still on course.
"Fake. Tankers destined for the US continue on course," Dmitriev said on X, linking to the FT story.
Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said detail of shipments were a "commercial" matter that could not be made public.
"All diesel will find its buyers," he added, without elaborating.
A third vessel was still in the North Atlantic headed toward the US but changed its destination from New York to a vague "for orders," without listing an unloading point.

Despite the fact that the US Treasury Department temporarily authorized Russian diesel transactions, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill warned port and terminal operators to turn away ships carrying the fuel.
In a letter earlier this week, she warned that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.”
Sherrill accused the Trump administration of lacking authority in overriding the import ban enacted by Congress more than four years ago.
She said New Jersey would act to prevent state facilities and companies from handling Russian fuel.
In a letter dated October 27, Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal warned shipping companies against violating US sanctions forbidding imports of Russian fuel.
"No president can unilaterally override a statute. Trump's license will not absolve you of legal and moral accountability," the letter read.

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s power grid on Saturday left more than 600,000 without electricity in the Dnipropetrovsk region in southeast Ukraine, electricity provider DTEK said on social media.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Sunday morning denounced “an overnight attack on the Dnipro region” that left energy infrastructure damages, also pointing out wider attacks across the country.
“There are widespread power outages across the country … Repair work is underway in virtually every affected city and community.”

The blackout follows shelling in the region on Nov. 3 that damaged infrastructure in a key industrial region bordering active combat areas, and a wider attack the same day across Ukraine targeting energy facilities.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant also lost power overnight, with the International Atomic Energy Agency saying on Sunday morning it is now relying “on emergency diesel generators for reactor cooling and other essential nuclear safety and security functions.”
The attack comes as Kyiv and Moscow gear up for another round of US-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi next week. Following the new wave of attacks on Saturday night Zelenskyy called on international partners to ramp up sanctions on Russia to hamper its capability to acquire or build more missiles.
“It is very important that they be synchronized across Europe and G7 jurisdictions. If the world does not have enough anti-ballistic capabilities to protect Ukrainian skies, then the missiles must be stopped on the production lines,” he said.

_In the final instalment of a four-part Health Matters wellness series on frontier medicine in Hong Kong, Elizabeth Cheung examines a dual-arm surgical robot that could remove gastrointestinal tumours in about half the usual time, and the hurdles between its first human trials and wider patient access._

Ho Man-wai underwent a colonoscopy in late August, during which doctors identified three polyps that needed to be removed before they could develop into cancer.

Two were removed during the initial examination, but the third was more deeply rooted and required a more complex procedure.

Ho, a 52-year-old property management worker, returned to hospital in September for an endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), a technique used to remove larger or more difficult polyps through an endoscope.

His polyp was relatively small, so the procedure took about an hour and Ho was discharged the following day.

But removing a polyp or a lesion measuring 3cm (1.2 inches) to 4cm can take up to two hours, according to Professor Philip Chiu Wai-yan, dean of medicine at the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK), who performed Ho’s procedure.

A new surgical device, developed under Chiu’s leadership, could cut the operating time for lesions of a similar size by half, to an average of 49 minutes.

Chiu, an internationally renowned surgeon, performed the world’s first robotic ESD in the stomach in 2011 and the world’s first such procedure in the colorectum in 2020.

[Video 5](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kw_ohPAO_Zc)

CUHK team demonstrates new EndoR Surgical System

The new device, known as the EndoR Surgical System, is designed to carry out the procedure more quickly and safely. It primarily targets patients with early-stage gastrointestinal cancers, or those with polyps that are difficult to remove.

The system consists of a long, thin tube that enters the body through a natural orifice, such as the anus or mouth, and performs surgery inside the gastrointestinal tract without making any incisions.

At present, it is the world’s only surgical robotic system equipped with two arms that can work throughout the entire gastrointestinal tract, and it has entered clinical trials.

Other surgical robots that enter through the body’s natural openings may not be able to reach some parts of the gastrointestinal system.

Chiu said the system’s robotic arms were what set it apart.

“The EndoR has two robot arms and they are really small,” Chiu said. “They have to perform this dissection with one arm for traction, the other arm is for dissection.”

The two arms, fitted with knife tips measuring just 1.5mm to 2mm, are housed inside the long, thin tube that also contains an endoscopic camera. The device enters the body and navigates the tortuous pathways of the gastrointestinal tract, sometimes travelling 70cm to 80cm from the entry point to reach the lesion.

The surgeon controls the robotic arms using two hand controls at a console.

Chiu said such precise, delicate arms were necessary because early-stage tumours were usually located in the mucosa, the innermost layer of the gastrointestinal tract.

To remove a tumour thoroughly, doctors must cut through the layer beneath it, known as the submucosa.

sources.title: Rosstat hack: data obtained suggests over 390,000 Russian deaths in Ukraine war | Euronews
sources.text: Advertisement By&nbsp Euronews Russian Published on 8 November 2026 - 18:04 GMT+1 Share Comments Add Euronews on Google Share Facebook Twitter Flipboard Send Reddit Linkedin Messenger Telegram VK Bluesky Threads Whatsapp Hacker groups Cyberpartisans BY and Silent Crow say they hacked Rosstat and counted Russian losses since the invasion of Ukraine. Their tally: between 393,000 and 450,000 killed. The hacker groups Kiberpartizany BY and Silent Crow claim to have carried out a large-scale breach of Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat). ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT According to the hackers, they managed to steal about 23 terabytes of data, including internal documents, demographic and economic statistics, as well as information on Russian losses in the war against Ukraine. The data obtained enabled the groups to make their own calculations of the number of people killed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. According to Kiberpartizany BY, as of 27 August 2026 at least 393,881 Russian citizens have been killed in the war. Silent Crow gives an even higher figure of 450,100 dead. This significant difference in estimates is due to the use of different methods of counting losses. Kiberpartizany BY counted deaths in which military action or its consequences were listed as the cause. Silent Crow, by contrast, not only included those killed in combat, but also added several other categories of deaths: non-combat losses among military personnel, deaths marked as terrorist acts, and deaths of people registered in Russia but who died in occupied territories or in Ukraine where the exact cause of death was not established. Why these figures are particularly important Russia has not released official statistics on combat losses since September 2022. In addition, from 2024 Rosstat stopped publishing annual data on causes of death, which has made an independent assessment of the demographic impact of the war much more difficult. Against this backdrop, access to the agency's internal statistical materials may make it possible to assess the scale of human losses more accurately. For comparison, as of 8 November the joint database of BBC News Russian Service and Mediazona, which collects a list of dead Russian servicemen identified by name, contained around 286,000 names. However, this list is known to be incomplete, especially for the most recent months of the war. In a joint study by Meduza and Mediazona, based on analysis of inheritance registry data, the number of fallen Russian servicemen by the end of 2025 was estimated at roughly 350,000. In this way, the hackers' estimates are in line with figures from previously published independent studies, although this does not yet prove the accuracy of each individual number. Verifying the authenticity of the data Meduza and Mediazona have said they obtained access to the data published by the hackers and have begun checking it. The journalists aim to establish not only whether the materials are authentic, but also how complete the information is they contain. In particular, they need to rule out the possibility of deliberate data falsification. Moreover, causes of death given in medical documents do not always reflect the actual circumstances of a person's death. It should also be noted that Rosstat's internal databases do not contain up-to-date information on people listed as missing. Such individuals may be declared dead only after a long period of time. Therefore even data from the state statistics agency cannot automatically provide a definitive figure for Russian military losses. If the authenticity and completeness of the leak are confirmed, the materials obtained could become one of the largest sources of information on the demographic consequences of the war for Russia. Keytruda After Kidney Cancer Surgery Lowers Risk of Death by 30%
Final KEYNOTE-564 data show Keytruda after kidney cancer surgery lowered the risk of death by 30%. Dr. Toni Choueiri explains what it means for patients.
Receiving Keytruda (pembrolizumab) after surgery for kidney cancer continued to help patients live longer and lowered the chance of their cancer coming back, according to the final analysis of the phase 3 KEYNOTE-564 trial presented at the 2026 ESMO Congress.
The trial included 994 patients with clear cell renal cell carcinoma at increased risk of recurrence after surgery to remove the kidney. After a median follow-up of about seven years, patients who received Keytruda had a 30% lower risk of death than those who received placebo. At seven years, 82.3% of patients who received Keytruda were alive, compared with 76.6% of those who received placebo. Keytruda also lowered the risk of the cancer coming back or death by 32%.
Keytruda, an immunotherapy that helps the immune system recognize and attack cancer cells, was approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2021 for this use. Treatment is given as an infusion every three weeks for up to about one year. No new safety concerns were identified with longer follow-up.
In an interview with CURE, Dr. Toni K. Choueiri, [title — verify], Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, explained what these findings mean for patients.
Choueiri: In an unselected population, because we do not have a biomarker yet despite our 20 years of shots on goal, [there are] patients who have a chance that the cancer comes back after [removing] the kidney because of micrometastatic disease that we cannot detect. Pembrolizumab will allow [these] patients to live longer by 30% and reduce the chance of the cancer coming back.
It’s not for everyone. We don’t know who it’s for, because surgery sometimes can cure patients alone. But with pembrolizumab, the chances of that cure are higher.

sources.text: Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Improves Outcomes in PD-L1-Negative Lung Cancer | CURE Advertisement News | Articles | November 4, 2026 Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Improves Outcomes in PD-L1-Negative Lung Cancer Fact checked by: Kaitlyn M. Le Patients with PD-L1-negative non-small cell lung cancer experienced longer progression-free survival with sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with chemotherapy plus Keytruda in a phase 3 trial. Advertisement Patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) who received sacituzumab tirumotecan (sac-TMT) plus Keytruda (pembrolizumab) had longer progression-free survival than those receiving chemotherapy plus Keytruda, according to findings from the phase 3 OptiTROP-Lung06 trial. The study, published in The New England Journal of Medicine , found that median progression-free survival was 15 months with sac-TMT plus Keytruda compared with 5.7 months with chemotherapy plus Keytruda. Progression-free survival refers to the length of time patients live without their cancer worsening or death from any cause. The combination reduced the relative risk of disease progression or death by 51%. However, overall survival data were not yet mature, meaning researchers have not determined whether the combination helps patients live longer overall. How Did Sac-TMT Plus Keytruda Affect Cancer Progression? The trial included 455 patients with previously untreated, locally advanced or metastatic nonsquamous NSCLC. All patients had PD-L1-negative tumors, meaning fewer than 1% of their tumor cells expressed PD-L1, and lacked targetable genomic alterations. PD-L1 is a protein that can help cancer cells avoid detection by the immune system. Patients with PD-L1-negative tumors may be less likely to benefit from immunotherapy alone. Chemotherapy plus Keytruda is a commonly used first-line treatment for these patients. Researchers evaluated whether replacing chemotherapy with sac-TMT, an antibody-drug conjugate designed to deliver cancer-fighting medication to cells expressing the protein TROP2, could improve outcomes. Norway's junior ice hockey team has been dropped from the World Junior Championship in Canada to make room for Russia, following a Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling ordering Russian teams to be reinstated in international competition. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Norway, which ranked 10th, has been moved to Division 1A to free a place for Russia at the tournament, which runs from 26 December to 5 January in Alberta. Tickets for the event, including for Norway's matches, are already on sale. The International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) has yet to formally confirm the change. Norway remained listed as a participant on the IIHF website on Monday. Russia's participation is also uncertain. The Russian team has not been guaranteed visas to enter Canada, which could restore Norway's place. "The situation is still unclear," Norwegian Ice Hockey Federation general secretary Petter Salsten said in a statement. Salsten said the federation disagrees with the CAS ruling but is obliged to comply. He added that the situation "clearly illustrates all the practical difficulties and immediate consequences for everyone involved if countries are immediately reinstated in full."

Six countries, including Norway, have pledged to boycott matches against Russia for as long as the war in Ukraine continues. Several long-standing corporate sponsors of ice hockey have also said they will withdraw support if Russia is allowed to compete.

Ukraine, which qualified for the senior men's championship for the first time since 2007, could be displaced if Russia is reinstated, as the lowest-ranked team would have to give way.

Russia: Independent Novaya Gazeta shuts its Moscow newsroom Skip to content
Launched in 1993, Novaya Gazeta often took on Russia's criminal and political elites Image: AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement The Novaya Gazeta newspaper closed its Moscow office on Monday, saying it was not able to continue reporting amid a campaign of state pressure in Russia .
The investigative outlet, co-founded by late USSR chief Mikhail Gorbachev, had long been a thorn in the Kremlin's side. In recent years, it ran into increasing roadblocks amid its critical coverage of the Russian invasion of Ukraine .
It was branded a "foreign agent," a Soviet-era term resuscitated by President Vladimir Putin 's administration, with officials ordering it to vacate its Moscow offices.
Russian banks were also forbidden from processing donations from readers and supporters. The paper had been heavily dependent on this income stream after moving wholly into online publishing, with the transition taking place shortly after the invasion of Ukraine. Russian authorities introduced new wartime censorship rules in the wake of the full-scale invasion.
Nobel Prize winner Muratov calls for free speech
2021 Nobel Peace Prize -winning founding editor Dmitry Muratov issued an appeal for free speech in wartime Russia as journalists gathered in the Novaya Gazeta offices to witness its closure.
"Those in our country who advocate for peace have been denied the right to read what they choose, as we see happening today," he said. "We are currently at a point where the section of the Russian constitution that guarantees political and civil rights has ceased to function."
Russia's government meanwhile sought to play down the significance of the closure, with Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying it was part of a "rotational process" in a fiercely competitive media landscape.
Novaya Gazeta was a flagship for post-Soviet democratic Russia and the era of "glasnost" or openness, also launched by Mikhail Gorbachev. The reformist Soviet leader used some of the prize fund for his 1990 Nobel Peace Prize as seed money for the publication.
The paper has built a reputation for fearless reporting, which has also put it in the crosshairs of Russia's wealthy and powerful. Six of its journalists were murdered since the paper was launched in 1993.
They included Anna Politkovskaya , who spent years investigating allegations of abuses by Russia's military during its campaigns in Chechnya. An early critic of Putin, she was found dead in her apartment bloc on the president's birthday in 2006.
Images published in Russian media on Monday showed the paper's editor-in-chief, Sergei Sokolov, taking down photographs of Polikovskaya and other reporters murdered in what's thought to be retribution for their work.
Last month, when first announcing that the paper would close, Sokolov said the outlet had "been killed." The paper was shutting down after "the Russian authorities — the Russian special services — have forced the editorial team to end its work," he said.
Will closure in Moscow mark a definitive end?
Muratov called for a ceasefire in Ukraine and urged foreign observers to remember the strength of dissent that endured in Russia, even if it was being pushed underground by censorship laws and other repression or intimidation.
"We canot blame the citizens themselves for this," Muratov said, "especially the wonderful, truly remarkable younger generation."
"I urge you to distinguish between the Russian authorities and the Russian people," he added.
Muratov also called for the release of around 4,000 people he termed political prisoners in Russia.
Novaya Gazeta 's leadership has not made it entirely clear whether its closing down in Moscow marks a defeinitive end to the outlet's reporting, or whether they might perhaps seek to regroup and begin operating in some form from outisde Russia , as several other publications including DW have been forced to in recent years.

New trilateral talks on Ukraine war: What to expect? Skip to content
Observers don't expect quick progress from the fresh talks Image: Dmytro Smolienko/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance Advertisement A new round of trilateral talks between Russia , Ukraine and the United States are scheduled to take place in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, months after a flurry of US-mediated peace talks earlier this year in January and February went nowhere .
When announcing the new trilateral talks last week, US special envoy Steve Witkoff said the discussions would focus on "post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, humanitarian efforts, and next steps toward peace."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has named security guarantees, an energy ceasefire, unblocking the Black Sea, extended prisoner exchanges, and preparations for a meeting of the leaders of Ukraine, the United States and Russia as his key topics.
Lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a member of Ukraine's delegation, told DW he was not expecting quick progress.
"I don't think there will be a breakthrough, after there was such a long break in the negotiation process," he said. "Simply the fact that trilateral talks are being resumed can be counted as a success."
Witkoff will be joined by US President Donald Trump 's son-in-law, real estate developer Jared Kushner, who serves as special envoy.
The Kremlin has sent Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to Russian President Vladimir Putin , to act as chief negotiator, along with a delegation including high-ranking Russian military and intelligence officials.
The Ukrainian delegation will be led by Rustem Umerov, head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service, along with Arakhamia, and diplomatic and military officials.
Separate formats are planned with several European representatives.
These include Günter Sautter, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's foreign and security policy adviser, Emmanuel Bonne, head of the Elysee Palace's diplomatic service and Jonathan Powell, the UK's national security advisor, and Fabrizio Saggio, diplomatic adviser to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Björn Seibert, Chief of Staff for the President of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and Geoffrey van Leeuwen, Chief of Staff for NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, will also attend.
It's doubtful, however, whether European representatives will be formally involved in talks on a potential peace deal.
Hanna Shelest, a security studies director at the foreign policy network Ukrainian Prism, told DW she believed they'd play "an observing role, at best."
She added that, until now, Russia had been reluctant to have European representatives at the table to uphold the impression that talks were "a matter between two superpowers" — namely, Russia and the United States — and to increase pressure on Washington.
"I doubt the Russian delegation will let the Europeans have a say," she told DW.
"Experience from the past years has taught us that as soon as Medinsky heads negotiations, the point becomes demonstrating to the US that Russia is willing to talk, but in reality, they won't reach an agreement," she explained. "Instead, there will be a long sermon about history and all sorts of other things."
However, she said Moscow sending high-ranking intelligence officers as part of the delegation was a "fairly positive aspect" of Russia's intentions.
She believed that additional negotiations were possible at this level.
This could include over prisoner exchanges or humanitarian pauses in villages near Oleshky, a town in the Russian occupied Kherson region in Ukraine's south, where US First Lady Melania Trump was credited with arranging a temporary truce in late October that secured humanitarian aid and allowed civilians to evacuate.
But despite these "positive signals," Shelest cautioned against hoping for concrete results, and suspected Russia was using the talks to stall.

Huang led Nvidia's transformation from a gaming chipmaker into a central supplier of AI technology (FILE: 21/10/2026) Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Shareholders sued chipmaker Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, on Monday, accusing them of concealing his alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset .
The proposed class action adds to investigations into whether Huang was targeted by foreign intelligence, raising questions about the security of sensitive information at the world's most valuable chipmaker.
The complaint, filed in federal court in San Jose, California, alleges that Nvidia and Huang misled investors about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed who is not related to him.
Shareholders say the defendants failed to disclose national security concerns that threatened Nvidia's reputation and business prospects. They are seeking unspecified damages.
The New York Times reported last month on the alleged relationship and said US authorities had concluded that Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia announced an independent investigation Sunday into reports that Huang had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort."
Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in an open letter, but did not identify the woman.
Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," he said. "I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security."
Nvidia shares closed down 4.3% Monday. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after US markets closed.
How have Washington and Beijing responded?
US President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating the matter, while expressing support for Huang.
Trump said he had spoken to the executive earlier that day.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump told reporters.
China denied conducting an intelligence operation targeting Huang.
"The so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.
Why does the case matter for the AI industry?
Huang co-founded Nvidia and led its transformation from a maker of gaming chips into a leading supplier of the computing technology powering artificial intelligence .
Its advanced chips have become a focus of US-China competition, with Washington restricting exports to limit Beijing's access to the technology.
Huang has pushed for looser restrictions on sales to China. The investigations have intensified scrutiny of his leadership and whether confidential company information was compromised.

There is no sign of an end to fighting in Ukraine despite US-brokered talks being held for the first time since February. ( AP: Evgeniy Maloletka )
Envoys from Kyiv, Moscow and Washington DC discuss security guarantees, territorial concessions and a Europe-wide security framework at their first meeting since February.
Despite Donald Trump insisting a deal can be done, the trilateral failed to provide any breakthroughs.
There remain major gaps between Ukraine and Russia on the terms of any possible agreement.
Russian and Ukrainian officials have met in Abu Dhabi for their first US-brokered talks since February, after Donald Trump suggested last week that a broad deal was possible on ending the war in Ukraine and guaranteeing security in Europe.
US envoy Jared Kushner told delegates that recent contacts with both sides had "really identified, narrowed the gaps", and the US side had "some good ideas" on how to bridge their differences.
Mr Trump, he said, was committed to achieving peace.
"He really has asked us to put extra effort into trying to find a solution that hopefully ends the war but also leaves both sides in a much stronger position" to realise their full potential, Mr Kushner said.
Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, is leading the trilateral talks with Russia and Ukraine. ( Reuters: Rula Rouhana )
But more than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and with Russian forces holding about a fifth of the country, Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart — despite Mr Trump's optimism — on terms for a possible settlement.
Ukraine's chief delegate, Rustem Umerov, said in his opening remarks that Kyiv was focused on achieving security guarantees and a lasting peace.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov underlined Moscow's preference for negotiating a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war.
"The idea of defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russia-Ukraine conflict, is absolutely reasonable," he told reporters in Moscow.
A day before the talks, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen voiced the opposite view, saying wider security talks should come only after a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Mr Lavrov again rejected the notion of a truce, saying the Europeans were trying to buy breathing space for Ukraine.
The new American drive for a deal has galvanised European officials into pushing for a place at the table to seek an end to the continent's deadliest conflict since World War Two.
Before the start of the main meeting, the Ukrainians met separately with European, NATO and EU representatives and the two American envoys, Mr Kushner and Steve Witkoff.
France said there could be no lasting peace in Ukraine without addressing European security, and that this required the involvement of the Europeans.
Rustem Umerov says Ukraine is unwilling to concede territory without serious security guarantees from allies. ( Reuters: Rula Rouhana )
Russia had made clear it did not see a place for Europeans at the meeting with the Ukrainians and Americans.
Describing the talks in Abu Dhabi as "very productive", US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the goal at some point was to expand the trilateral talks to include the Europeans.
The US president has frequently said an agreement was close, without a deal emerging.
However, negotiations have picked up again in recent weeks after months in which Washington's attention was focused on the war in Iran.

letters.subject: Source request: Cancer drug deals and R-Pharm payments
letters.body:
Dear ICIJ team,

PLAIN. is an independent, advertising-free Swiss news site reporting internationally. Our investigative desk is looking into pharmaceutical payments to a Russian distributor with corruption allegations, including contracts, beneficial ownership, state-linked actors, and effects on patients and legitimate distributors. This research is AI-assisted and every text is reviewed by a human editor.

1. Can you confirm the date and contractual basis of Merck’s 2009 strategic alliance with R-Pharm to sell Keytruda to the Russian government, and identify the documents relied on?
2. What evidence supports the account that Alexey Repik founded R-Pharm in 2001 after selling his car and borrowing $15,000 from his mother?
3. Which specific Federal Antimonopoly Service decisions or case dates found that R-Pharm coordinated bidding or engaged in anticompetitive conduct to maintain high drug prices and influence contract winners?
4. What evidence links the offshore company connected to Alexey Repik to the Bombardier business jet apparently used by one of Vladimir Putin’s daughters?
5. Which whistleblower documents show that Merck, Eli Lilly, Novartis and AstraZeneca paid Russian distributors excessive sales bonuses and rebates of 15% to 35%, and how was the international average of rarely exceeding 10% calculated?

We will publish your reply, in full or summarized as you prefer. Please tell us if any statement above is factually wrong. We would appreciate an answer by 11 November 2026.

PLAIN. Investigative desk
desk@plain-news.ch

letters.subject: Investigative inquiry: Payments to Russian distributor R-Pharm and beneficial ownership structures
letters.body:
Dear Merck & Co.,

PLAIN. is the investigative desk of plain-news.ch, an independent, advertising-free Swiss news site. Our research is AI-assisted and every text is reviewed by a human editor. We are investigating how pharmaceutical companies paid millions to a Russian distributor with corruption allegations to win cancer drug business, tracing the payments, contracts and beneficial ownership behind the distributor.

We request the following:

1. The exact dollar amounts and dates of payments Merck made to R-Pharm or any proxy or intermediary between 2009 and 2022.
2. The findings of Merck's internal investigation into alleged bid-rigging or anticompetitive conduct involving R-Pharm, and any enforcement actions or penalties that resulted.
3. The identities and beneficial ownership structures of any proxies or intermediaries that received payments on Merck's behalf in connection with Russian state contracts for Keytruda.
4. The outcomes, penalties or enforcement actions resulting from Russia's Federal Antimonopoly Service investigations into R-Pharm.

We will publish your reply; you may choose full or summarized. Please correct anything factually wrong. We ask for an answer by 13 November 2026.

PLAIN. Investigative desk
desk@plain-news.ch
